vignette:
# Margaret's Story

Margaret sits with her hands folded in her lap, a habit she's developed over the past three years. At sixty-seven, she carries herself with the composed bearing of someone who has spent four decades working in nonprofit management—first in education advocacy, then in refugee services. Her colleagues have always described her as steady, reliable, the kind of person who keeps things running even when everything feels chaotic. She still goes to work most days, though lately she wonders if anyone has noticed how much less she participates in meetings.

The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn three years ago. Margaret had stayed late at the office to finish grant proposals, something she'd done hundreds of times before. The building was nearly empty when she walked to her car in the parking garage. A man emerged from between two vehicles, and what followed was a blur of violence and terror that lasted perhaps fifteen minutes but has somehow stretched across every day since.

She reported it to the police. She pressed charges. She attended the trial. He was convicted. By most measures, the system worked. Yet Margaret finds herself unable to shake the feeling that the assault never really ended—it simply transformed into something that lives inside her now.

The physical recovery was straightforward enough. The psychological aftermath has been far more stubborn. Margaret startles at unexpected sounds, her body flooding with adrenaline before her mind can catch up. When a colleague touches her shoulder to get her attention, she flinches violently enough that it causes embarrassment. She's learned to position her desk so she can see the door of her office at all times. She no longer uses the parking garage; instead, she parks on the street and walks an extra block, even in rain.

Sleep has become a negotiation. Margaret lies awake for hours, her mind cycling through what-ifs and worst-case scenarios. When she finally does sleep, she often wakes gasping, her sheets soaked through, with no clear memory of the nightmare that jolted her awake. Her husband, Rajesh, has become accustomed to sleeping in the guest room. He tries to be understanding, but Margaret can see the worry etched into the lines around his eyes, the way he hesitates before approaching her.

At work, Margaret has pulled back from the community engagement that once energized her. The nonprofit serves vulnerable populations—many of them trauma survivors themselves—and she finds herself unable to listen to their stories without becoming overwhelmed. A client's account of violence last month left her shaking in the bathroom for twenty minutes. She called in sick the next day, something she almost never does.

The intrusive thoughts are relentless. She'll be reviewing a budget spreadsheet when suddenly she's back in the parking garage, her heart hammering against her ribs. The smell of diesel fuel from a delivery truck outside her office window sends her spiraling. She's hyperaware of her body in ways that feel both protective and imprisoning—constantly monitoring for threat, never quite believing she's actually safe.

Margaret knows intellectually that the assault is over, that the man is in prison, that statistically she is safe. But her nervous system hasn't received this memo. It remains convinced that danger is imminent, that vigilance is the only thing standing between her and catastrophe. She moves through her days with a kind of grim determination, showing up to work, maintaining her marriage, going through the motions of a life that feels increasingly distant from who she used to be.
